common_name: G21085 Hardy Hibiscus (Early-Blooming Dark Red-Blue Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Set container plants out after the soil has warmed in spring; this selection breaks dormancy and flowers up to a month earlier than typical hardy hibiscus, so mark the crown location since it emerges later than most other perennials nearby.

directions: Plant in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun, since this cultivar comes from a breeding line selected for earlier emergence and bloom than standard hardy hibiscus. Flowers open dark red with cool blue overtones and a dusky, greyed-purple eye, with minimal petal veining, on a compact, densely branched plant with chocolate-brown to violet young foliage that greens with age. Cut the dead stems to the ground after frost and expect a tidy, upright mound roughly 3 to 3.5 feet tall and wide at maturity.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent USPP36695P2 (granted May 20, 2025), inventor Richard A. Grazzini, assignee Garden Genetics LLC

common_name: G21086 Hardy Hibiscus (Compact Cherry-Red Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Set container-grown plants out in spring once the soil has warmed; this compact selection stays under 4 feet, making it a fit for smaller beds than older large-growing hardy hibiscus.

directions: Grow in consistently moist, fertile soil in full sun to support heavy midsummer-to-fall flowering. Cherry-red 6 to 7 inch blooms show a red eye only slightly darker than the petals, with distinct veining radiating outward, above chocolate-brown to dark violet young foliage that matures to green. The plant forms a dense, upright, well-branched mound with 5 to 8 basal shoots, staying more compact than many older moscheutos hybrids. Cut stems to the ground after frost each winter and expect late spring emergence typical of the species.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent USPP36673P2 (granted May 13, 2025), inventor Richard A. Grazzini, assignee Garden Genetics LLC

common_name: G21087 Hardy Hibiscus (Compact Veined Light Pink Perennial Hibiscus)

planting.note: Plant container-grown crowns in spring in rich, evenly moist soil; this selection emerges roughly a month earlier than typical hardy hibiscus and produces more basal shoots than its parent line.

directions: Plant in moist to wet, fertile soil in full sun, watering through dry spells to keep flowering steady. Large 6 to 8 inch light pink flowers are marked by a prominent red eye and distinct dark veins radiating across the petals, set against foliage that opens deep purple and matures to a chocolate-brown to dark violet cast. The compact, densely branched habit and earlier-than-average emergence make it a candidate for gardeners wanting an earlier start to the hardy hibiscus season. Cut stems to the ground after the first hard frost each winter.
sources: U.S. Plant Patent USPP36750P2 (granted June 17, 2025), inventor Richard A. Grazzini, assignee Garden Genetics LLC
